transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-03-15 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (SE), Priya (Redwood), Daniel (HelixPay), Sasha (HelixPay PM), Rita (HelixPay Security)

Summary:
High-level POC scoping call to align on HelixPay's integration path for Redwood. Focus areas: using Redwood's OpenAI-compatible endpoints versus native SDKs, support for function/tool calling and structured JSON output, benchmarks for latency and throughput, and security/private deployment concerns. Agreed to run a 2-week benchmark window in early April and exchange security artifacts.

Topics covered: success criteria, workload sizing, benchmarks, SDK options (Python/Node/Go), streaming vs non-streaming, function calling/tooling, structured output (JSON schema enforcement), private deployment (VPC/KMS/SOC2), rollout plan and timeline.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro: I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this, Liam is our SE, Priya is joining for integration questions. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Daniel (HelixPay): Good, thanks Maya. We're excited to scope this POC — we want to replace a brittle rule engine for payment routing with an LLM-assisted decision layer.
[00:15] Sasha (HelixPay): Hi, yeah, goal is to prototype a decision assistant that suggests routing options and flags potential fraud patterns. success criteria are both quality and latency.
[00:23] Liam (Redwood): Cool. quick clarifying q: when you say latency, are you referring to end-to-end API latency from your service to our hosted endpoint or internal processing including your enrichment steps?
[00:32] Daniel: End-to-end as perceived by our users — so the LLM call needs to be under about 200 to 300 ms p95 for short responses, but for the initial POC we're flexible as long as we can demonstrate < 500 ms p95.
[00:43] Maya: that's useful. we can do incremental targets — POC goal: p95 < 500ms on a hosted Redwood instance, milestone for Dedicated: p95 < 250ms at 50 QPS with 128-token outputs.
[00:56] Rita (HelixPay): security is a big deal — we need SOC 2 certs, audit logs, and customer-managed keys. Also data residency is something to consider — we operate in us-east for payments.
[01:10] Priya (Redwood): to align — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem packages if you need air-gapped. For hosted we provide SOC 2 artifacts and audit logs; for Dedicated we can offer VPC peering and restricted IP ranges.
[01:24] Sasha: can you explain the difference between OpenAI-compatible endpoints and the Redwood SDK? we have some code that already talks to openai.com endpoints.
[01:32] Liam: yes. Redwood exposes two main integration surfaces: 1) OpenAI-compatible endpoints — same request/response shapes as OpenAI's API so minimal code changes; 2) Native Redwood SDKs that add higher-level features (streaming helpers, built-in retry/backoff, batching helpers, and built-in structured output validators). The compatibility layer is effectively a translation shim; most customers prototype on OpenAI-compat then move to native SDKs for production.
[01:56] Daniel: perfect. we prefer to avoid large refactors, so starting with openai-compat is attractive. any caveats with feature parity — e.g., function calling or tool invocation?
[02:06] Liam: function calling is supported on the OpenAI-compat surface too, but there are caveats: we support the basic function calling contract, but complex multi-tool orchestrations are better handled via our SDK where you get helpers for schema enforcement and structured output. Also note streaming function-call tokens may interleave differently depending on quantization — sometimes transcript shows odd token boundaries — it's a small gotcha.
[02:30] Sasha: on structured output — we need deterministic JSON output for downstream parsers. can Redwood enforce schema and validate/repair output?
[02:38] Priya: yes, Redwood has structured output features — you can provide a JSON schema and Redwood will run a validator and return a structured payload or a validation error. There's also an optional auto-repair layer that attempts to fix JSON issues, but for strict compliance we recommend SDK-based post-process checks.
[02:55] Daniel: what about streaming? our UI expects to show incremental suggestions as tokens come in. Is streaming supported on the compat endpoint?
[03:02] Liam: streaming is supported on both surfaces. There are two streaming modes: chunked streaming for low-latency first-byte, and delimited streaming for more deterministic JSON assembly. For structured output we often recommend using delimited streams so your front-end can assemble a valid JSON progressively.
[03:20] Sasha: excellent. next, benchmarks: we need to size for a peak of ~30 QPS initially, plan for 60 QPS if the pilot succeeds. We also need guidance on batch sizes and token limits.
[03:32] Liam: for the initial model profile — if you target 128-token averages for completions, 30 QPS maps to roughly X tokens per second; we'll include a spreadsheet but rough guidance: continuous batching helps throughput but increases latency variance. For low-p95 latency you want smaller batch windows and possibly Dedicated with GPU pooling.
[03:50] Daniel: can you give a realistic example number: if we run hosted on a mainstream open model what p95 can we expect?
[03:56] Liam: depends on model. For mid-sized 7B-style models on optimized GPU path, hosted Redwood can hit ~120-200ms p95 for 64-token responses in a favorable profile. For larger 13B+ models expect 200-400ms. These are rough; the benchmark run will give exact numbers with your prompt mix.
[04:16] Rita: from security — any concerns about sending de-identified traces? we need guarantees on retention and deletion.
[04:23] Priya: we have per-customer retention config and auto-delete policies. For POC we recommend you share masked traces; we can also set up an ephemeral benchmark instance in your VPC if you prefer not to send data off-site.
[04:40] Sasha: timeline question — what's a realistic POC length and milestones?
[04:44] Maya: typical POC: 4 to 6 weeks. Week 0: SOW and infra prep. Week 1-2: benchmark window + data collection. Week 3: model tuning, structured output schema validation, run end-to-end integration test. Week 4: wrap, handoff and decision. We can shrink to 3 weeks if you limit scope to one model and hosted infra.
[05:02] Daniel: okay good. For success criteria we propose: 1) functional parity — structured output meets schema on 95% of sample prompts; 2) p95 latency < 500ms for hosted during peak test; 3) throughput target of 30 QPS sustained with less than 5% error rate. Thoughts?
[05:19] Liam: those are sensible. Let's add a quality threshold for routing decisions — e.g., human-in-the-loop accuracy target on a labeled set. We can compute precision/recall on sample decisions.
[05:29] Sasha: yes we can provide labeled decisions. We'll also want a fallback: if the model doesn't meet threshold, route to rule engine.
[05:36] Maya: that's a good safety net. We'll include canary traffic and a fallback policy in the SOW.
[05:42] Rita: about keys and KMS — for Dedicated or Private we need HSM-backed KMS. Is that available?
[05:49] Priya: yes for Private/on-prem we support HSM integrations. For Dedicated we offer bring-your-own-KMS with customer-managed keys in a supported cloud KMS and strict rotation policies. We'll include the KMS integration doc.
[06:02] Daniel: can you talk a bit about cost expectations for a POC vs Dedicated? we need rough ops numbers to budget.
[06:09] Maya: rough hosted POC cost is usage-based — we'll provide a sample pricing sheet. Dedicated has monthly commit costs but reduces per-token unit cost for sustained workloads. For benchmarking you'll see the cost delta; we'll include a cost model spreadsheet that shows token volume, batch efficiency improvements, and projected monthly spend.
[06:28] Liam: one more technical detail — KV cache and prefix caching. If you have repeated contexts (like customer profile blobs) we can cache KV between requests to reduce compute; you'll need to send a stable cache key. That can cut token compute by 30-60% depending on your repetition.
[06:48] Daniel: nice. on the SDK languages — we primarily use Java/Node in our microservices. any examples in Java or Node?
[06:54] Priya: we currently ship maintained SDKs for Python, Node and Go. There's a community Java client we can point to and sample wrappers for Microservices. For immediate POC you can use the OpenAI-compat HTTP calls from Java; we'll also provide Node samples that map to the compat API and to native Redwood helpers.
[07:11] Sasha: what about tool/function calling orchestration — we have multiple downstream services (risk scoring, price check). can Redwood trigger multiple tool calls atomically?
[07:20] Liam: Redwood's function calling supports invoking named tools and returning structured data. For multi-tool orchestration we recommend the SDK orchestrator which sequences calls, enforces timeouts and supports compensating actions. There isn't an atomic distributed transaction — that must be composed by your orchestration layer. We can provide pattern docs.
[07:38] Daniel: ok, pattern docs will help. Also we need to validate that outputs don't leak sensitive tokens. Is there PII redaction options?
[07:45] Priya: we have built-in PII detection hooks and optional redaction during logging/retention. For extra safety we recommend client-side masking before sending, and we'll also enable server-side redaction for any logs retained by Redwood.
[07:59] Sasha: benchmark specifics — Liam, can you talk about the inputs you need from us to run benchmarks?
[08:05] Liam: we'll need: 1) ~200 representative prompts including edge cases; 2) an average token length estimate for prompt and completion; 3) a small set of labeled decisions for quality eval; 4) expected peak QPS and concurrency profile; and 5) whether you'll run in hosted or VPC/dedicated. We'll share a spreadsheet template.
[08:22] Daniel: we can do that. Also, for the benchmark, can we test both OpenAI-compat and native SDK paths to compare overhead?
[08:29] Liam: absolutely. we'll spin up two identical test harnesses and run the same workload against the compat endpoints and a native SDK path — measure latency, token efficiency, error rates, and assembly time for structured output.
[08:42] Maya: we'll also capture telemetry for per-token cost and include cost comparisons in the final benchmark report.
[08:49] Rita: about audit logs — we need immutable audit trails with user/email, request metadata, and redaction markers. Is that in the product?
[08:57] Priya: yes — audit logs include request/response hashes, user identity (SSO), timestamps, and retention controls. For Private we can ship logs to your SIEM. For Hosted we can integrate with your cloud logging securely.
[09:12] Sasha: are there any known limitations with function calling schema size or nesting depth?
[09:18] Liam: very deep nesting can cause larger tokens; the integrator side usually flattens payloads. We recommend modestly nested JSON schemas and explicit field types. We'll provide best-practice examples.
[09:30] Daniel: great. let's talk about success metrics in the SOW text — quality, latency, throughput, error budget and rollout criteria.
[09:36] Maya: agreed. SOW will include concrete numeric thresholds: structured output schema pass rate >= 95%, p95 latency thresholds as discussed, less than 2% API error rate during benchmark, and a go/no-go decision gate.
[09:51] Sasha: who will be the touchpoints on the Redwood side during the POC?
[09:55] Maya: primary AE is me, SE is Liam, Priya will help with SDK and structured output. We'll give you a dedicated slack channel and SRE channel for the benchmark window.
[10:05] Daniel: perfect. one more Q on logs — how quickly can you rotate keys if we request key rotation?
[10:10] Priya: for hosted we support on-demand rotation with a 24-48 hour window for re-encrypting caches; Dedicated we can do more quickly depending on your KMS flow. We'll document the process.
[10:22] Sasha: ok timeline recap — Maya, you'll send SOW/pricing by Mar 17; Liam sends benchmark plan by Mar 19; HelixPay to provide prompts and traces by Mar 20; benchmark week Apr 6-8.
[10:36] Maya: yes that matches my notes.
[10:39] Daniel: sounds good. small note — we might request a short deep-dive on function calling orchestration with your SEs during week 2.
[10:46] Liam: happy to do that — we can schedule a 60-minute technical session focusing on tool orchestration and SDK patterns.
[10:53] Rita: final question from compliance: if we run the benchmark in your hosted environment, can logs be set to auto-delete after 7 days?
[11:00] Priya: yes, retention is configurable per-project; we'll set it to 7 days for the POC and document that in the SOW.
[11:09] Sasha: thanks all. any other open items?
[11:12] Maya: none from our side. we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the benchmark.
[11:17] Daniel: thanks. appreciate the clarity.

End recap (quick bullets):
- POC scope: validate structured output for payment routing, measure latency/throughput and compute cost tradeoffs.
- Benchmarks: run hosted vs native SDK comparisons during Apr 6-8.
- Success criteria: schema pass rate >=95%, p95 < 500ms (hosted POC), throughput 30 QPS sustained, <5% error rate.
- Security: Redwood to provide SOC2 artifacts, PII redaction options, KMS integration docs, and retention config (set to 7 days for POC).
- Owners: Maya (SOW/pricing), Liam (benchmark plan), Daniel (prompts & traces), Rita (security questionnaire).
